new_statements.quote: Some observations about word stress and intonational stress: 1. In Western Tamang the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word. 2. Intonational stress on the last syllable of a word before a phrase juncture or sentence final can be quite intense and change the pattern. This variation, however, is conditioned by higher level intonation factors.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word. It is realised by intensity on the onset consonant and vowel of the stressed syllable plus slight lengthening of the syllable's closing element, not by pitch (pitch is the exponent of the four word-tones); the authors warn that the tense mid-rising tone contour makes the second syllable sound more prominent to an untrained ear.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. A separate 'intonational stress' falls on the last syllable of a word before a phrase juncture or sentence end and can be intense (adds high pitch, rises/falls, crescendo), but is attributed to intonation, not word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('always'). Caveat p. 116-117: perceptual deception by the tense mid-rising contour on bi-/trisyllables, and contours with sharp falls sounding more heavily stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word/morpheme with its tone); phrase-final prominence is explicitly assigned to intonation. Tone language with four word-tones (tense high-falling, tense high-level, lax mid-falling, lax low-level). Later Nuwakot-based work (Regmi 2019, Nepalese Linguistics 34: 46) says only 'The stress is not distinctive in Tamang', consistent with fixed stress; Mazaudon (2005, 2014) says for Eastern/Risiangku Tamang that all syllables are about evenly stressed.
new_statements.identity_note: nort3144 is not a distinct entity: [tmk] was an Ethnologue/Varenkamp-survey code for the Nuwakot central-strip (plus Dhading) portion of Western Tamang. Ethnologue 17/22 locate tmk in 'Nuwakot district, central mountainous strip' (94% lexical similarity with Western Trisuli Tamang [tdg]); Glottolog's nort3144 point (27.91N 85.16E) sits at Trisuli Bazar. The SIL survey that motivated the merger (Lipp 2014, p. 14) used Sahugaun, Nuwakot as its [tmk] site. The quoted statement describes Sahugaon/Sahugaun, 'some five miles north-northwest of Trisuli Bazar in Nuwakot District' (Varenkamp 1996 p. 42: 27deg58'N 85deg04'E) -- i.e. the same variety, and the SAME source and passage the catalog already uses for Western Tamang west2415 (ISO tdg). Ethnologue's tdg entry conversely labels the Dhading dialect 'Northwestern' and puts Trisuli (Nuwakot) under tdg, and Glottolog 5.3 has a separate dialect node 'Northwestern' [nort2711] under west2415, so the tmk/tdg boundary was never coherent. Recommend folding nort3144 into the existing west2415 entry rather than counting a second language; do not double-count.

II.C Stress, p. 116: 'In Western Tamang the basic word stress falls always on the first syllable of a word'; intonational stress on the phrase-final syllable is conditioned by intonation; word stress is intensity + slight length, not pitch. Dialect: Sahugaon, ~5 miles NNW of Trisuli Bazar, Nuwakot District (p. 2).
